posts.title: The analytics existed before the post did

copy.default:
One of the more useful things I found while rebuilding how I learn from LinkedIn was not a winning hook.

It was bad evidence.

Eleven analytics snapshots in the old learning pool had refresh timestamps from before the posts were actually due to publish.

If I had trusted the dashboard blindly, those snapshots could have taught the system that good posts failed before anybody had even seen them.

So I changed the rule.

A post now has to be independently verified as published, old enough to have meaningful data, and refreshed after publication before it gets a vote.

That sounds like a content problem.

It is really an operating principle.

Bad data does not become useful because it is automated.

The faster the system learns, the more important it is to make sure it is learning from something true.

posts.title: I would rather leave the slot empty

copy.default:
I have changed one rule in how I think about content:

An empty slot is better than a weak post.

For a while, the tempting goal was simple.

Keep Buffer full.
Keep publishing.
Keep the machine moving.

But volume can hide a quality problem.

If the only reason a post exists is because there was space on the calendar, the calendar has started making the strategy.

I would rather the system say:

“We have room, but nothing here is strong enough yet.”

Then create something better.

That is the same principle I increasingly like in client work too.

Automation should remove avoidable effort.

It should not remove judgement.

posts.title: The lead did not disappear when they enquired

copy.default:
The lead did not disappear when they enquired.

They disappeared somewhere after that.

That distinction matters.

If somebody raised their hand, there was already intent.

So before blaming lead quality, I want to know what happened next.

How quickly did they get a useful response?
Was the next step obvious?
Did they know what to expect?
If they did not book, was there a sensible second contact?
Did anybody record why the conversation ended?

“More leads” is an acquisition answer.

Those are journey questions.

And if the leak is happening after intent already exists, spending more at the top can make the underlying problem more expensive rather than solving it.

An automated process can still be unowned.

That is one of the easiest ways for it to decay.

The messages are sending.
The workflow is active.
Nobody is obviously responsible for it.

Then a link changes.
A staff handoff changes.
The booking process changes.
A segment stops behaving the way it used to.

Nothing technically “breaks” enough to trigger panic.

The system just becomes less useful.

For every automation I increasingly want one simple answer:

Who owns the outcome this automation is supposed to create?

Not who built it.

Who notices when reality changes?

Automation removes repeated manual work. It does not remove accountability.

A client can be completely satisfied and still not come back.

That sounds contradictory until you think about how people actually behave.

They leave happy.
They plan to book later.
Work gets busy.
The reminder never comes.
The normal return window passes.

Nothing went wrong with the service.

The relationship still decayed.

That is why I do not think retention should be reduced to “make customers happier”.

Experience matters enormously.

But so do timing, memory, friction and the clarity of the next step.

A good return system is not there to rescue a bad service.

It is there to stop a good service being forgotten.

posts.title: Most follow-up problems are classification problems

copy.default:
A lot of follow-up problems are really classification problems.

The business knows somebody has not booked.

But it does not know what kind of “not booked” they are.

New enquiry waiting for an answer?
Interested but comparing options?
Cancelled appointment?
No-show?
Past client now overdue?
Former regular who has been gone for a year?
Already booked somewhere else in the system?

Those are not one audience.

So “send a follow-up” is not enough of an instruction.

First classify the customer state.

Then decide whether contact is useful, what it should help with, and what action should stop it.

Better messaging often starts before the writing.

posts.title: A good diagnosis can recommend doing nothing

copy.default:
I want 222Emails to be able to tell a business:

“Do nothing here.”

Not every gap deserves another automation.
Not every dormant customer is recoverable.
Not every quiet week has a retention cause.
Not every enquiry should be chased.

Sometimes the realistic value is too small.
Sometimes the data is not usable.
Sometimes the process already works.
Sometimes the real constraint is somewhere else entirely.

That is why I keep coming back to diagnosis before delivery.

Find the leak.
Understand the mechanism.
Estimate whether fixing it is commercially meaningful.

Then earn the right to recommend a system.

A solution is more credible when “no solution needed” is genuinely allowed to win.

posts.title: Revenue Recovery is not a win-back blast

copy.default:
Revenue Recovery is not another name for sending a win-back campaign to everybody who has not bought recently.

The job starts earlier.

Which commercial moment was missed?

An enquiry that stalled.
A cancellation that never recovered.
A no-show with no return path.
A client who passed their normal rebooking window.
A former regular who became dormant.

Those states have different causes, different timing and different next actions.

A blanket campaign treats them as one problem.

A recovery system tries to understand the state first, then decides whether contact is appropriate and what should happen next.

posts.title: The six parts of a return system

copy.default:
A useful client return system needs more than a reminder.

Six parts matter:

1. State
What just happened?

2. Timing
When does the next action become useful?

3. Message
What uncertainty or friction should be reduced?

4. Route
What is the easiest appropriate next step?

5. Stop rule
What event means the system should stop?

6. Measurement
How will the business know whether the journey improved?

Skip the first two and automation becomes noise.

Skip the stop rule and it becomes annoying.

Skip measurement and nobody knows whether it worked.

posts.title: Follow-up needs ownership, not just automation

copy.default:
A follow-up process can be automated and still be operationally weak.

The missing piece is often ownership.

Who notices when the booking journey changes?
Who checks that the right people still enter the workflow?
Who owns a conversation once a staff member steps in?
Who updates the route when an offer or service changes?
Who reviews whether the system is producing the intended outcome?

Automation should reduce repetitive work.

It should not create a process that everybody assumes somebody else is watching.

A gap in the diary does not automatically require a discount.

Sometimes the better question is whether there is existing intent that has not been connected to the available capacity.

Recently cancelled clients.
Warm enquiries that never completed a booking.
Clients genuinely due to return.
People who asked about a relevant service and paused.

The objective is not to manufacture urgency or broadcast to the whole database.

It is to identify whether an appropriate customer state already exists, then make the next step easier.

Price is one lever.

Timing and relevance are others.

posts.title: What the Revenue Recovery Check is allowed to say

copy.default:
A Revenue Recovery Check should be allowed to produce three different answers.

1. There appears to be a meaningful recovery opportunity.

2. There may be an opportunity, but more evidence is needed before recommending a build.

3. There is nothing here we can responsibly justify fixing right now.

That third answer matters.

A diagnostic becomes much less useful if every path ends at the same sale.

The purpose of the check is to reduce uncertainty around missed enquiries, weak follow-up, no-shows and lapsed clients.

The implementation has to earn its way into the recommendation.

Retention School: Event vs state

An event is something that happened.

A state is what is true now.

Examples:

Event: appointment cancelled.
State: cancelled, not yet rebooked.

Event: first visit completed.
State: first-time client, not yet returned.

Event: enquiry submitted.
State: interested, not yet booked.

Why does this matter?

Because good lifecycle automation should usually respond to the current state, not blindly react to an old event.

The event tells you where the customer came from.

The state tells you what job exists now.

Retention School resource: Stop-rule checklist

Before switching on a follow-up journey, ask:

Does it stop when the customer books?
Does it stop when a staff member takes ownership?
Does it stop after an explicit no?
Does it stop after an opt-out?
Does it stop when the customer enters a different journey?
Does it stop after the commercial window has clearly passed?

Triggers get most of the attention because they start automation.

Stop rules protect the customer experience because they know when automation has finished its job.

Retention School: The human handoff

Automation should know when a person has taken over.

Imagine this sequence:

1. Customer enquires.
2. Automated acknowledgement is sent.
3. Staff member replies personally.
4. Automated chase continues anyway.

The automation is technically working.

The experience is not.

A clean handoff needs a rule that changes ownership or pauses the automated journey once human conversation begins.

The best automation is not the one that sends the most reliably.

It is the one that knows when it is no longer needed.

posts.title: Lesson: measure after the message has had time to work

copy.default:
Retention School: Measurement needs a maturity window

Do not judge a lifecycle message before the customer has had a fair chance to act.

A reminder sent five minutes ago has not failed because it has zero bookings.

A rebooking journey should be measured against the decision window it was designed for.

That means defining:

When the message is sent.
How long a reasonable response can take.
What outcome counts.
What comparison period is fair.

Fast dashboards make data visible quickly.

They do not make customer behaviour happen faster.

Retention School resource: Recovery opportunity matrix

Before building a recovery journey, score the opportunity on three dimensions:

1. Intent
How much evidence is there that the customer wanted the service?

2. Recency
How recently did the relevant event happen?

3. Value
Is recovering this state commercially meaningful?

High intent + recent + meaningful value:
Prioritise diagnosis.

Low intent + old + low value:
Probably not where to start.

The point is not to reduce every customer to a score.

It is to stop treating every missed interaction as equally recoverable.
